reviews.text: Trained and professional doctors with care for animals.

We've been treated at this clinic since 2022, as my Pomeranian suffers from epileptic seizures. The doctors have always cared for us and supported us in a very professional, competent, and empathetic manner. It's clear they're veterinarians who love dogs and their work. WELL DONE!

My dog ​​fainted after a blow to the side, and I took him to the nearest emergency room (9:30 PM). He's alive because I refused to euthanize him and hospitalize him: I took him home.
What I received was psychological terror: "He'll die in two hours, or tonight." Given that Giotto is 15 years old, he's undergoing treatment for heart disease, but he wants to live, he eats, and he's lively.
His enlarged spleen was interpreted as a burst tumor—either from the blow or from a burst mass—but without any biopsy to confirm it.
A message, as a customer: "He's dying anyway" should never be said to those who love their pet. We take our pets to the vet to save them; and when that's not possible, family members deserve to die at home, not hospitalized "under observation." What's the point of hospitalizing a terminally ill patient? And the painkiller, which I was told three times was "useless"? I had him give it anyway.

Today, Sunday, August 3rd: wake up at 7:00 a.m., walk in the countryside. A check-up revealed a spleen that wasn't perfect, but that of an elderly dog, no lesions, no fluid. He didn't bleed to death in two hours.

ANSWER TO HIS: "HER COLLEAGUE DID OTHER THINGS TOO, NOT JUST "I ​​HAVE TO DIE ANYWAY" REPEATED LIKE A BROKEN RECORD, BUT SHE TRIED TO CONVINCE MY SON TO CONVINCE ME TO SURRENDER TO AN WRONG AND FORCED DIAGNOSIS. YOU MAKE HYPOTHESES AND THEN RECOMMEND EUTHANASIA? I WOULD SAY VERY PROFESSIONAL! IT WAS AN EPILEPTIC SEIZURE, WHICH RESURRECTED EXACTLY A MONTH OLD, IT MADE HIM ILL FOR DAYS AND NO ONE TOLD ME TO END UP WITH HIM, THEY TREATED HIM AND TODAY HE IS RUNNING AND HAPPY AT 15 YEARS OLD. ARE YOU MOCKING ME FOR THE PHOTO? A MINUTE WITH A.I., SHE MUST COMMIT TO CHECKING WHO WORKS IN YOUR CLINIC.

I absolutely do not recommend this place. The night between Saturday and Sunday, my 16-year-old dog with vestibular syndrome (diagnosed three years ago) was sick, his teeth chattered violently, he was shaking, he vomited. We went immediately to the clinic where we were told that they could see him but for the neurologist we would have to wait until the next day, that is, Saturday. We were also told that Saturday and Sunday the neurologist is at the clinic on call and for the next day there were already two, with 3 of us, so we would have seen the neurologist without problems. We left, sleepless night waiting for the morning that never came. At 10, as recommended, we are at the clinic. At the reception I explain everything and I am asked to wait my turn. After about an hour and a half I went back to ask (I saw dogs and cats coming in and out after the visit and I was there with my dog ​​fasting and without drinking since the previous day because he would have vomited) I was told that entry was based on emergencies. I waited and waited and went back to ask saying, once again, that I had been there the previous night and that I had been told I had two patients in front of me, everything had passed me by and even my dog ​​was in an emergency, vestibular syndrome with widespread tremors throughout the body, vomiting and weakness 16 years old!!! I was told that none of the visits before mine had been neurological (false because I had asked a gentleman who had told me he was there for the neurologist) and in any case she would have gone to ask because evidently the doctors were closing the files. Around 1:40 pm I came back a little pissed off this time he told me he would follow up. At 2 pm they called me we went in, the first thing the vet asked me was the description of the person who gave me the information that night, I told him and he told me that this was not the case, the neurologist is NOT present in the clinic and he will examine my dog. I was exhausted we had the visit which did not address my fears (in fact we have an appointment elsewhere) I went out, paid €187.00 and asked the lady in reception why she kept me there for almost 5 hours without telling me that the neurologist was not present!!! She answered me candidly (for the first time because the previous times her manner had been poorly concealed condescending) that it was not about the absence of the neurologist!!! I won't go on; you can imagine I didn't keep quiet; I told them they were completely unfair! I forgot. In the meantime, a lady approached me and asked when the neurologist would be arriving. She replied, "At 2:30 PM, she's coming especially for you." You decide, if these people are serious. They tried to place the blame on the night nurse when in fact she was simply telling me the truth. The person who was unfair was the one who made me wait until 2 PM without informing me that I wouldn't be seeing a neurologist!!! Vestibular syndrome is an exclusively neurological disorder!!!
Very professional, they did everything and more to save my dog, even though unfortunately she passed away I am still satisfied with how she was treated.

On September 21, 2025, we arrived at the clinic in very serious condition. Amore had hemorrhagic gastroenteritis with bloody diarrhea, was severely dehydrated, and his tests showed significant changes. We were truly scared.
Thanks to the professionalism, promptness, and care of the doctors and all the staff, Amore was stabilized and treated in the best possible way. On September 24, 2025, he was finally able to come home with us. ❤️
Today, he is well, happy, active, and all of this is now just a bad memory. 🐾
I will never forget what you did for him. To us, Amore is more than just a dog; he is part of our family. Thank you for saving his life and for allowing us to have him home. ❤️

AWFUL EXPERIENCE: total lack of communication, unforgivable delays, and patient abandonment.

I strongly advise against this facility to anyone who loves their pet. We brought our cat here for tests, and, at their recommendation, a lymph node cytology was performed. We were promised a response by the next day.
The reality was a nightmare: the results arrived after two weeks of total silence, during which we sent dozens of emails and made constant phone calls to doctors and reception, without ever receiving a single response or update. Only after repeated phone calls, 14 days later, were we emailed the results. A vague report, which said everything and nothing, with no clear diagnosis, no instructions on how to proceed, and, above all, no one from the clinic ever contacted us to explain the situation or guide us. They literally left us to ourselves with a sick animal.
Desperate, we turned to other veterinarians who, immediately demonstrating empathy, tact, and true professionalism, repeated the cytology exam, immediately uncovering the truth: a highly aggressive lymphoma. Unfortunately, the time lost at the Tibaldi Clinic was fatal. We could have learned the truth and acted a month ago, sparing our cat weeks of unnecessary discomfort and managing the situation promptly. Instead, we received a definitive diagnosis only the very day we had to say goodbye to her forever, as she passed away yesterday.
If you're looking for a facility that treats patients with seriousness, respects promised timelines, and communicates with the owners, look elsewhere. Here, we found only indifference.

A very disappointing experience. I showed up on a Saturday evening for my dog's severe bloody diarrhea. I fully understand that more urgent cases can occur in a veterinary emergency room, so the wait itself wasn't the problem. What left me perplexed was seeing the doctor having considerable difficulty managing the situation while performing a simple blood test, so much so that we had to wait a long time for another colleague to arrive. My dog ​​is anxious and fearful and initially barks at strangers, but over the years, he has always been examined in our presence by various vets without any problems. On this occasion, too, he stopped barking as soon as the doctor entered the room. Despite this, we were offered the option of performing the test without our presence, a solution that has never been necessary in other facilities. What disappointed me most was the feeling of inexperience in caring for a frightened dog and the total lack of empathy when I expressed my concerns about the muzzle, given that my dog, at the mere sight of it, ran away and hid out of fear.
For a visit and blood test, we spent over €180. The cost may be in line with an emergency service, but personally, I would have expected professional handling. I'd also like to add, for Giotto's mother, if you're reading this, that I felt your pain that evening but didn't want to be intrusive; I'm glad Giotto is okay now.
I'd also like to add, in response to your comment on this review, that, as already mentioned, the procedure—the blood test—was performed by various professionals, without all the drama that occurred that evening. Furthermore, between the lines and politely, my message was different: that perhaps there wasn't the experience and professionalism required for a simple procedure; I don't want to imagine the rest. I know the ATS procedure and I assure you that there is a very precise assessment, so the dog is not immediately identified as a biter, especially if it reacts out of fear in a very specific context.
Furthermore, there is no scientific evidence demonstrating that changing operators facilitates blood sampling, so please let's not get ahead of ourselves. Thank you and never again.

There are doctors who treat illnesses and doctors who care for people and their animals. Dr. Amedeo Picchi belongs to this second, extremely rare category.

For months, he cared for our beloved Ercole, a French bulldog suffering from an extremely complex condition, accompanying us with impeccable professionalism, extraordinary availability, and profound humanity. He never deceived us, but he never made us feel alone. He explored every possible avenue, consulting with other specialists, respecting our every question, and sharing every decision with us.

In his final, extremely difficult days, he did everything medicine could offer. And when he realized that continuing would only prolong Ercole's suffering, he had the courage, sensitivity, and honesty to help us perform the most painful gesture a family can face, but also the greatest act of love.

Ercole was never a number, nor a simple clinical case. For Dr. Picchi, he was always Ercole. And this, for us, was the most authentic demonstration of the respect he has for every animal entrusted to his care.

His expertise is extraordinary, but what we will always cherish in our hearts is his compassion, his sincerity, his ability to be there even when there was no more care to offer, only dignity to protect.

A veterinarian can be very good. A doctor can be excellent. But being a person capable of accompanying a family through the most difficult time of their lives is an extremely rare gift.

On July 3, 2026, we said goodbye to our Ercole. That day, Dr. Picchi was by our side. He fought until the very end to save him, and when that was no longer possible, he gave him a peaceful departure, without suffering and with all the respect he deserved.

For this, we will be grateful to him forever.

Thank you, Dr. Picchi. We will never forget.

First of all, I'll summarize that my dog's diagnosis left no room for doubt, and reaching it was easy with the help of instrumental tests.

My veterinarian informs me that my dog's blood tests, which are very debilitated, have revealed severe anemia. She tells me to go to the emergency room for possible abdominal bleeding, which was confirmed by an ultrasound performed at Tibaldi, but which doesn't clarify the cause. The vet who took care of my brother-in-law suggested a CT scan to determine the cause and a one- or two-day hospital stay. He suggested possible poisoning, but also a mass in the spleen. Given the good blood test results, spleen removal might be considered (though I was skeptical, given my dog's 14-year history of joint pain, which is managed with monoclonal antibodies). But despite his kindness and occasional thoughtfulness, he was more focused on writing and commenting on the financial estimate than explaining what might follow the CT scan. He made no mention whatsoever of the possibility of euthanasia immediately after the CT scan while my dog ​​was still under sedation. I couldn't have known or even imagined it, but he did. He's a vet and had an obligation to inform me.

I agreed to be admitted to the hospital and undergo a CT scan, stressing that I wouldn't be leaving the waiting room, and that he would update me and call me before the sedation to say hello and reassure him. To avoid further anxiety, I lightly and cheerfully said goodbye to my big dog, petted him, and watched him enter the ward.

In the afternoon, a doctor informed me that the CT scan was underway, without anyone having informed me in advance as I had requested. She returned accompanied by the doctor who had performed the CT scan, who didn't explain to me what the results implied, what the consequences would be, and that, therefore, it would be best to euthanize the dog while he was still under sedation. He expressed himself this way: "Unfortunately, the news isn't good. The bleeding is coming from one of the masses found in the spleen and liver. We can put him to sleep now that he's already sedated." He then turned to his colleague, asking how the "clinic" was going, as if to confirm, demonstrating that, before suggesting euthanasia, he hadn't made any inquiries or bothered to fully assess the situation. He told me this in the conversational, lighthearted, and occasionally smiling tone of a livestock veterinarian informing me that the cow is fat and can be put down.

The way I was told this, brutal as it may be, had no impact on my dog's fate. BUT THAT HE CLOSED HIS EYES FOR THE LAST TIME TO UNKNOWN FACES IS A REGRET THAT WILL REMAIN WITH ME. Our story, which began in a shelter kennel, when I promised him I'd never leave him alone again, ended this way due to carelessness and indifference.
